communityOpportunitiesPendingManualPost.thread: Coding Agents Are Arguing. Hand Them the Same Playbook (2026-07-14, 2pts)
communityOpportunitiesPendingManualPost.whyGenuine: Directly about multi-agent convention drift; terminalblog's AGENTS.md Complete Guide is the concrete fix (which file each harness loads, how to prove it read it, OS pitfalls).
communityOpportunitiesPendingManualPost.suggestedReply: This is exactly the problem a shared instruction file solves — but the catch is each harness reads a different one (AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / .cursorrules) and silently ignores the others. We wrote the complete guide to doing it once and having every agent follow it, including the Windows/permission traps: https://terminalblog.com/blog/agents-md-complete-guide/

communityOpportunitiesPendingManualPost.thread: Cursor 0day: When Full Disclosure Becomes the Only Protection Left (2026-07-14, 14pts)
communityOpportunitiesPendingManualPost.whyGenuine: Security incident on a coding agent; terminalblog's Coding Agent Security Checklist 2026 is the operator hardening companion (sandbox, permissions, secrets, MCP egress, incident response).
communityOpportunitiesPendingManualPost.suggestedReply: The deeper lesson from this Cursor 0day: an agent is a process with a shell, your env vars, and network egress — not a chatbot. When it breaks it commits to main or leaks a token. We keep a runnable hardening checklist for exactly this, with a command to find your own holes: https://terminalblog.com/blog/coding-agent-security-checklist-2026/

communityOpportunitiesPendingManualPost.thread: AI won't take your job. You may get fired anyway (2026-07-14, 1pt)
communityOpportunitiesPendingManualPost.whyGenuine: Process-readiness angle; terminalblog's 'Most Teams Aren't Ready for What Coding Agents Do Next' covers the review-throughput / deploy-gate / credential gaps specifically.
communityOpportunitiesPendingManualPost.suggestedReply: The 'you'll get fired anyway' framing misses the real bottleneck: it's not whether the agent writes code, it's that your review and deploy process can't absorb 10 agent PRs a day. That's a process gap, not a model gap. We broke down what teams need to fix first: https://terminalblog.com/blog/teams-not-ready-for-coding-agents/

communityOpportunitiesPendingManualPost.suggestedReply: Nice — this is the audit layer more teams need. It pairs with the boring-but-essential hardening: least-privilege permissions, denying reads on credential paths, and gating MCP egress. We keep the full runnable checklist here: https://terminalblog.com/blog/coding-agent-security-checklist-2026/

communityOpportunitiesPendingManualPost.thread: Cursor user wondering if Claude Code is worth switching to (HN item 47619702 / 47622041)
communityOpportunitiesPendingManualPost.whyGenuine: The thread keeps circling 'which tool is cheaper/better.' terminalblog's real-cost piece reframes it to the actual lever (token meter + context waste + retry storms), which is genuinely useful and not self-promotional in tone.
communityOpportunitiesPendingManualPost.suggestedReply: Switching tool X to Y won't fix your bill — the subscription is the decoy, the token meter is the real cost. A single messy refactor can burn $5–30, and an agent stuck in a retry loop re-sends your whole context window every attempt. The people who come out ahead set token caps and scope context; they don't necessarily pick a different IDE. We wrote up the costs that never show on a pricing page: https://terminalblog.com/blog/real-cost-of-ai-coding-agents/
